options: Preclean, penetrant/dwell, remove excess, develop, inspect, postclean
Penetrant first, then preclean, then inspect, then develop it all here now
Develop first, then inspect, then penetrant, then preclean it all here now
Remove excess first, then penetrant, then develop, then preclean here now
content.explanation: The standard order is precleaning, penetrant application and dwell, excess removal, developing, inspection, and postcleaning.
distractors: Precleaning must come first, before penetrant.
This reverses the entire sequence.
Excess removal cannot precede penetrant application.

content.stem: Spray application of developer is preferred to be:
options: Even and light to avoid masking fine indications
Heavy and fully pooled up thick here oddly
Applied well before any penetrant here somehow
Fully skipped on all the small parts here somehow
content.explanation: An even, light developer coat preserves the visibility of small indications; pooling or heavy coats can hide them.
distractors: Heavy pooled developer masks indications.
Developer always follows penetrant and removal.
Developer is needed on small parts too, except where a no-developer technique is specifically qualified.

content.stem: Inspection must be completed within the development window because, given too much time:
options: Indications may over-bleed and blur, hurting interpretation
Nothing at all really changes here, somehow quite oddly
The whole entire part fully magnetizes up itself here, oddly
The dry developer turns right into the red penetrant here, oddly
content.explanation: Excessive development time lets indications spread and blur, so viewing occurs within the specified window for reliable interpretation.
distractors: Indications do change over time; they can over-bleed.
There is no magnetization in PT.
Developer does not convert into penetrant.

content.stem: Fixtures and baskets that contact penetrant should be cleaned because residual penetrant can:
options: Transfer to parts and cause false indications
Greatly improve the overall sensitivity too here
Act just like a dry developer here, somehow oddly
Magnetize the whole parts fully right here oddly
content.explanation: Penetrant left on fixtures can smear onto parts, producing false indications, so handling equipment is kept clean.
distractors: Contamination harms, not improves, results.
Residual penetrant is not a developer.
There is no magnetization in PT.

content.stem: Tighter, finer discontinuities generally require:
options: Longer penetrant dwell to fill the small openings
A much shorter penetrant dwell time setting here somehow
No penetrant dwell time at all here somehow
A much higher UV-A lamp power setting here
content.explanation: Fine, tight openings fill more slowly, so longer dwell times are specified to ensure adequate penetration before removal.
distractors: Shorter dwell risks under-filling tight cracks.
Some dwell is always required.
UV power affects viewing, not penetration into tight cracks.

content.stem: Skipping postcleaning can be a problem because residues may:
options: Cause corrosion or interfere with later coating, bonding, or service
Greatly improve the whole part's fatigue life here, quite oddly
Greatly increase the sensitivity of all the future tests here, quite oddly
Magnetize the whole entire part fully right here, quite oddly
content.explanation: Leftover penetrant and developer can corrode the part or impair downstream processes and service, so postcleaning is performed when required.
distractors: Residues do not improve fatigue life.
Residues do not enhance future test sensitivity; they can interfere.
There is no magnetization in PT.

content.stem: The biggest risk during excess penetrant removal is:
options: Over-removal that strips penetrant from discontinuities
Adding far too much red penetrant onto it all here oddly
Magnetizing the whole entire part fully right here oddly
Drying the whole part out far too slowly right here
content.explanation: Over-removal pulls penetrant out of the openings, weakening or erasing indications, so removal is controlled to clear only the surface background.
distractors: Removal takes penetrant away; it does not add it.
There is no magnetization in PT.
Slow drying is a separate concern, not the main removal risk.

content.stem: Water-wash pressure for removing water-washable penetrant is typically limited to about:
options: 40 psi or less
150 psi
500 psi
Pressure does not matter
content.explanation: Wash pressure is commonly held to about 40 psi or less to avoid driving water into openings and over-removing penetrant; the specification gives exact limits.
distractors: 150 psi is well above typical wash limits and risks over-removal.
500 psi would aggressively strip penetrant from openings.
Pressure strongly affects removal control, so it does matter.

content.stem: Water-wash temperature is controlled (commonly roughly 50 to 100 degrees F) because temperature affects:
options: Removal effectiveness and penetrant behavior
The exact UV-A light wavelength used here
The whole part's overall magnetism level here
The dry developer's outer color shade here
content.explanation: Wash water that is too hot or cold changes removal behavior and can harm sensitivity, so a moderate controlled temperature range is used.
distractors: Wash temperature does not change UV wavelength.
There is no magnetism in PT.
Wash temperature does not set developer color.

content.stem: Water washing is best done with a:
options: Coarse spray at a controlled angle and distance
A high-pressure jet aimed right into the openings
A long soak down in still, standing water here too
A hot, high-pressure steam blast here somehow
content.explanation: A coarse, controlled spray removes surface penetrant without forcing water into openings; aggressive jets or steam can over-remove.
distractors: A high-pressure jet into openings drives out trapped penetrant.
A long still soak does not effectively remove surface penetrant and can dilute it.
A steam blast is too aggressive and can over-remove and bake residues.

content.stem: When washing fluorescent penetrant, removal is best monitored:
options: Under UV-A so the inspector can see background being removed
In total, complete darkness with no light at all here oddly so
Under bright white room light only here, quite oddly
Without any viewing light at all here, quite oddly enough
content.explanation: Washing under UV-A lets the operator watch the fluorescent background disappear and stop before over-washing.
distractors: Total darkness prevents seeing the wash progress.
Bright white light hides the fluorescent background being removed.
Some illumination (UV-A) is needed to monitor the wash.

content.stem: For a lipophilic (Method B) emulsifier, the most critical control is:
options: Emulsification (contact) time before washing
The dry developer's particular outer color shade here
The UV-A lamp's total wattage rating here
The whole part's overall measured weight
content.explanation: Lipophilic emulsifier diffuses into the penetrant over time; too long lets it reach penetrant in openings and over-remove, so contact time is tightly controlled.
distractors: Developer color is unrelated to emulsification control.
UV wattage is a viewing parameter, not an emulsification control.
Part weight does not control emulsification.

content.stem: Lipophilic emulsifier is typically applied by dipping and then:
options: Allowed to act undisturbed for the timed period (no agitation)
Vigorously scrubbed hard all over the whole surface here oddly
Sprayed off hard at high pressure all over here, somehow oddly
Wiped down hard with a wet solvent cloth here somehow oddly
content.explanation: The lipophilic emulsifier is left to diffuse without agitation for a controlled time; scrubbing or spraying would force it into openings and over-remove.
distractors: Scrubbing drives emulsifier into openings and over-removes.
High-pressure spray disturbs the controlled diffusion.
Solvent wiping is the Method C technique, not lipophilic emulsification.

content.stem: Hydrophilic (Method D) removal usually begins with a:
options: Pre-rinse to remove most surface penetrant before the remover bath
A quick solvent dampened cloth wipe down here, really quite oddly enough
A dry, loose developer powder dusting all over here, quite oddly
A full UV-A black light exposure all over it here, quite oddly
content.explanation: A water pre-rinse knocks down the bulk of surface penetrant, reducing the load on the hydrophilic remover and improving control and consistency.
distractors: A solvent wipe is the Method C technique, not the hydrophilic sequence.
Dry powder is a developer, not a removal step.
UV exposure is for viewing, not removal.

content.stem: Hydrophilic remover is used at a controlled concentration because too high a concentration can:
options: Over-remove penetrant from discontinuities
Improve sensitivity without any real limit at all
Greatly increase the dye's fluorescence here somehow
Magnetize the whole entire part fully right here
content.explanation: An overly concentrated hydrophilic remover acts too aggressively and strips penetrant from openings; concentration and contact time are controlled to the specification.
distractors: Higher concentration does not endlessly improve sensitivity; it can degrade it.
Concentration does not increase fluorescence.
There is no magnetism in PT.

content.stem: Hydrophilic remover may be applied by:
options: Immersion (dip) or spray at controlled concentration
Only ever by simple dry brushing here, quite oddly
Only ever by simple solvent wiping here, quite oddly
Only ever by full UV-A light exposure here, oddly
content.explanation: Hydrophilic remover is applied as a dip bath or as a spray, each at a controlled concentration appropriate to the method.
distractors: Dry brushing does not apply a liquid remover.
Solvent wiping is Method C, not hydrophilic removal.
UV exposure does not remove penetrant.

content.stem: The cardinal rule of solvent (Method C) removal is to:
options: Wipe with a solvent-dampened cloth, never flush solvent onto the surface
Spray the wet solvent directly straight into all the openings here, oddly
Soak the whole entire part right down deep in wet solvent here oddly
Use just plain water only on it here at all, somehow quite oddly
content.explanation: Flushing or spraying solvent on the part washes penetrant out of the openings; correct practice is wiping with a clean cloth, then a lightly solvent-dampened cloth.
distractors: Spraying solvent into openings removes the trapped penetrant.
Soaking the part in solvent dissolves penetrant out of openings.
Method C uses solvent, not water, for removal.

content.stem: Correct solvent removal uses:
options: A dry wipe first, then a separate solvent-dampened wipe
One single heavy wet solvent flood all over here, oddly
Only a single dry cloth used here at all, quite oddly
Only plain running water used here at all, quite oddly
content.explanation: Removing most excess with a dry cloth, then lightly wiping with solvent, minimizes the chance of leaching penetrant from the openings.
distractors: A heavy solvent flood over-removes.
A dry cloth alone leaves a penetrant film that needs light solvent wiping.
Water is not used in Method C removal.

content.stem: Over-washing or over-emulsification typically results in:
options: Weak, missing, or faded indications
Heavy red dye background only here
Much brighter, stronger indications
Much faster developing overall here
content.explanation: Removing too much penetrant from openings leaves little to bleed back, so indications are weak or absent; the cure is better-controlled removal.
distractors: Over-washing reduces background, not increases it; the problem is lost indications.
Over-washing dims, not brightens, indications.
It does not speed development; it impairs detection.

content.stem: Insufficient removal (under-washing) typically results in:
options: Excessive background that masks indications
No real background at all here, oddly
Much sharper, cleaner indications here
A full loss of all the red penetrant dye here
content.explanation: Leaving surface penetrant produces heavy background that hides true indications; the surface must be cleaned of excess while preserving trapped penetrant.
distractors: Under-washing leaves more, not less, background.
It blurs rather than sharpens indications.
Under-washing leaves too much penetrant, not too little.

content.stem: The fundamental tension in the removal step is between:
options: Removing enough background and not removing penetrant from discontinuities
Just the process speed and the dye color here at all, somehow quite oddly so
Just the penetrant dwell time and the dry developer here, quite oddly
Just the UV-A light and the bright white light here at all, quite oddly
content.explanation: Good removal clears background while preserving trapped penetrant; pushing too far either way degrades the result, which is why removal is controlled.
distractors: The core tension is about how much penetrant is removed, not speed and color.
Dwell and developer are separate steps from removal control.
UV versus white light is a viewing choice, not the removal tension.

content.stem: Post-emulsifiable methods resist over-washing better than water-washable because:
options: The penetrant is not water-removable until the emulsifier is applied
They simply use no water at all in them here at all, quite oddly
They need no dry developer at all here at all, somehow quite oddly enough
They are always the visible color dye type only here, quite oddly
content.explanation: Until emulsified, the penetrant cannot be washed off by water, so the operator controls exactly when and how much removal occurs, protecting penetrant in openings.
distractors: Post-emulsifiable methods still use water in the wash step.
A developer is still required.
Post-emulsifiable penetrants can be fluorescent or visible.

content.stem: If emulsifier is left on too long, it can:
options: Diffuse into discontinuities and allow trapped penetrant to wash out
Greatly improve the final indication retention here, quite oddly
Have no real effect at all on any of the openings here, quite oddly enough
Greatly increase the whole penetrant dwell time here, quite oddly
content.explanation: Excess emulsification time lets the emulsifier reach penetrant inside the openings, making it water-removable and lost during washing.
distractors: Excess emulsification reduces, not improves, retention.
It does affect the openings by enabling over-removal.
Emulsification time is distinct from penetrant dwell.

content.stem: Wash water that is too hot can:
options: Promote over-removal and dry penetrant in openings
Have no real effect on it at all here, quite oddly
Greatly increase the overall sensitivity here
Greatly improve the overall contrast here too
content.explanation: Hot wash water can be too aggressive and can dry penetrant in the openings, both reducing indications, so temperature is controlled.
distractors: Wash temperature does affect removal and sensitivity.
Excess heat degrades, not increases, sensitivity.
It does not improve contrast; it can reduce indications.

content.stem: Penetrant carried out of the tank on parts and fixtures (drag-out) is a concern for:
options: Material economy and contamination control
The applied magnetic field strength level here
The exact UV-A light wavelength used here
The dry developer's outer color shade here
content.explanation: Drag-out wastes penetrant and can contaminate downstream baths, so it is managed by drainage and good handling.
distractors: Drag-out has nothing to do with magnetism.
It does not affect UV wavelength.
It is not about developer color.

content.stem: Removal of visible penetrant excess is judged by:
options: Inspecting the surface under white light for residual background
Inspecting it only under the UV-A black light here, quite oddly enough
Weighing the whole entire part on a scale here, quite oddly
Measuring the whole part's magnetism level here, quite oddly
content.explanation: For visible penetrant, the operator checks under white light that the colored background is removed while the openings retain penetrant.
distractors: Visible penetrant is judged under white light, not UV.
Part weight does not indicate removal adequacy.
There is no magnetism in PT.

content.stem: Using a cloth that is soaked (dripping) with solvent for removal is wrong because it:
options: Acts like flushing and leaches penetrant from openings
It dries the whole part out far too slowly here, oddly
It adds even more red penetrant right onto it here oddly
It fully magnetizes the whole wiping cloth here, oddly
content.explanation: A dripping solvent cloth behaves like flushing, dissolving penetrant out of the openings; the cloth should be only lightly dampened.
distractors: The issue is over-removal, not slow drying.
Solvent wiping removes, not adds, penetrant.
There is no magnetism involved.

content.stem: The pre-rinse in hydrophilic removal serves to:
options: Remove the bulk of surface penetrant before the controlled remover step
Apply the whole dry developer coating right onto it here, quite oddly
Fully dry out the whole entire part surface here at all, quite oddly
Add the emulsifier right down into all of the open openings here oddly so
content.explanation: Pre-rinsing lowers the surface penetrant load so the hydrophilic remover can finish removal in a controlled, consistent way.
distractors: Pre-rinse is a removal step, not developer application.
It wets rather than dries the part.
It is meant to remove surface penetrant, not drive emulsifier into openings.

content.stem: In a hydrophilic dip remover, mild agitation is used to:
options: Assist uniform, controlled removal of surface penetrant
Force the remover right down into the openings here, oddly
Heat up the whole remover bath right up hot here, oddly
Add even more bright fluorescence right into it here oddly
content.explanation: Gentle agitation promotes even removal across the surface; excessive agitation or concentration risks over-removal.
distractors: Agitation should not be so aggressive as to drive remover into openings.
Agitation is not for heating the bath.
Agitation does not add fluorescence.

content.stem: Holding the wash nozzle too close to the part can:
options: Over-remove penetrant from openings
Improve the indication retention here
Have no real effect at all here oddly
Reduce the background too little here
content.explanation: A close, concentrated stream acts aggressively and can wash penetrant out of openings; distance and angle are controlled.
distractors: Close washing reduces, not improves, retention.
Nozzle distance clearly affects removal aggressiveness.
Too-close washing removes too much, not too little.

content.stem: Hydrophilic remover concentration is verified during process control by:
options: Measuring concentration (for example, by refractometer) against the specified value
Just reading off a magnetic field gaussmeter from it here, somehow quite oddly
Just weighing the whole entire part on a big scale here at all, quite oddly
Just timing the whole dry developer dwell with a stopwatch here, quite oddly now too
content.explanation: Remover concentration is checked (often with a refractometer) and adjusted to stay within the specified range for controlled removal.
distractors: A gaussmeter measures magnetic field, irrelevant to PT.
Part weight does not indicate remover concentration.
Developer timing is a separate control.

content.stem: Solvent removal is well suited to field work because it:
options: Needs no water supply or tanks
It cannot ever over-remove here
It detects the deep subsurface defects
It requires a full dark room here oddly
content.explanation: Method C requires only cloths and solvent, making it portable; however, careful wiping is needed to avoid over-removal.
distractors: Improper solvent technique can over-remove.
PT does not detect subsurface defects.
Visible Method C does not require a darkroom.

content.stem: After water-based removal, the next step before a dry or nonaqueous developer is to:
options: Dry the part appropriately
Reapply the penetrant again
Apply the emulsifier all again
Skip right ahead to inspection
content.explanation: The washed part is dried (within temperature limits) so dry or nonaqueous developer can form a proper film; aqueous developer may be applied before drying.
distractors: Penetrant is not reapplied after removal.
Emulsifier is not reapplied after washing.
Inspection follows development, not removal.

content.stem: If over-emulsification has stripped penetrant from a discontinuity, the inspector should:
options: Clean and reprocess the part from the penetrant step
Just add on even more dry developer here, oddly
Just greatly increase the UV-A lamp power here
Just accept the whole part fully as is here, oddly so
content.explanation: Lost penetrant cannot be restored by later steps; the part must be cleaned and reprocessed from penetrant application to obtain valid indications.
distractors: Developer cannot replace penetrant that was washed out.
More UV does not recover lost penetrant.
Accepting the part risks missing real defects.

content.stem: Wash water and spent remover are managed as:
options: Process effluent requiring proper handling/disposal
Just plain clean drinking water here, somehow oddly
Just more dry developer powder here, oddly
Just more red penetrant kept aside for reuse here
content.explanation: Spent process fluids are handled and disposed of per environmental and safety requirements; they are not reused as fresh materials.
distractors: Process effluent is not potable.
Spent fluids are not developer.
Contaminated fluids are not reused as fresh penetrant.

content.stem: Uneven removal across a part can cause:
options: Inconsistent background and unreliable interpretation
A perfectly uniform brightness all over here, oddly
Far better overall contrast all over everywhere here too
No real effect at all on it here at all, oddly
content.explanation: Patchy removal leaves some areas with background and others over-removed, undermining consistent interpretation; removal is applied evenly.
distractors: Uneven removal produces uneven, not uniform, results.
It worsens, not improves, contrast consistency.
Uneven removal does affect the result.

content.stem: On a rough as-cast surface, water-washable penetrant is prone to:
options: Trapping in surface texture, causing high background or over-washing attempts
Somehow detecting the deep buried subsurface porosity too here, quite oddly now
Fully eliminating the whole dry developer step entirely here, quite oddly now
Fully magnetizing the whole entire casting part here, somehow quite oddly now
content.explanation: Rough surfaces hold penetrant in the texture, so the operator faces background that tempts over-washing; post-emulsifiable or careful technique helps.
distractors: PT does not detect subsurface porosity.
A developer is still required.
There is no magnetization in PT.

content.stem: Emulsifier and remover baths have controlled temperature because temperature affects:
options: Removal rate and consistency
The exact UV-A wavelength here
The whole magnetic field here
The dry developer's color here
content.explanation: Bath temperature changes how fast emulsification/removal proceeds, so it is controlled for repeatable results.
distractors: Bath temperature does not change UV wavelength.
There is no magnetic field in PT.
It does not set developer color.

content.stem: Adequate rinsing after removal is verified by checking that:
options: Surface background penetrant is gone while openings retain penetrant
The whole entire part is fully magnetized up here, quite oddly enough
Every last bit of the penetrant is fully gone here, somehow quite oddly
The whole dry developer coating is fully applied on here, quite oddly
content.explanation: The rinse is judged complete when background is removed without stripping the openings; this balance defines proper removal.
distractors: There is no magnetization in PT.
Removing all penetrant, including from openings, would erase indications.
Developer application is a later, separate step.

content.stem: Solvent removers used in Method C should be:
options: Compatible with the penetrant family and the part material
Just any old household cleaner at all here, quite oddly enough
Just plain water always, in every single case here, quite oddly
Just a strong acid always, in every single case here, quite oddly
content.explanation: Removers are part of a qualified family and must be compatible with the penetrant and not harm the part; arbitrary cleaners can degrade results or damage parts.
distractors: Arbitrary household cleaners are not qualified for the process.
Method C uses solvent, not water.
Strong acids would damage parts and are not solvent removers.

content.stem: Spraying wash water straight into a discontinuity is avoided because it:
options: Can flush penetrant out of the opening
It improves the penetration here oddly
It adds even more red penetrant in here
It dries out the whole opening here oddly
content.explanation: Direct, forceful water into an opening washes out the trapped penetrant, so washing is done at an angle with controlled pressure.
distractors: Penetration is done; washing into openings removes penetrant.
Washing removes, not adds, penetrant.
The concern is removal of penetrant, not drying.

content.stem: The removal step is often considered the most skill-dependent because it:
options: Directly controls the balance between background and indication strength
It sets the whole red penetrant's chemistry here at all, quite oddly
It determines the exact UV-A light wavelength needed here, quite oddly so
It fully magnetizes the whole entire part here at all, quite oddly
content.explanation: How the operator removes excess decides whether background is clean and whether indications survive, making it the most judgment-intensive step.
distractors: Penetrant chemistry is set by the material, not the removal step.
UV wavelength is fixed by the lamp, not removal.
There is no magnetization in PT.

content.stem: Compared with water-washable penetrant, hydrophilic post-emulsifiable processing generally gives:
options: Better control and higher achievable sensitivity
Far less overall control here, quite oddly
No real need for any water at all here, oddly enough
Far lower overall sensitivity, always, here
content.explanation: Separating penetration from removal (via the remover step) gives more control and supports higher sensitivity than self-emulsifying water-washable penetrant.
distractors: It offers more, not less, control.
Hydrophilic processing still uses water.
It does not inherently mean lower sensitivity; it often supports higher.

content.stem: Emulsification time and remover concentration are:
options: Controlled and recorded process parameters
Just left to the operator's own whim here oddly
Fully irrelevant here, somehow quite oddly
Just set by the dry developer alone here
content.explanation: These parameters are specified, controlled, and documented because they strongly affect removal and sensitivity.
distractors: They are controlled, not arbitrary.
They are highly relevant to results.
The developer does not set emulsification parameters.

content.stem: After washing fluorescent penetrant, a quick check under UV before developing can confirm:
options: That background is adequately removed before proceeding
The exact deep crack depth down inside of it here, oddly enough
The whole entire part is fully magnetized up here
The dry developer's outer color shade here, oddly
content.explanation: A UV check after washing confirms the surface background is clean enough to proceed to developing; remaining background may require careful additional washing.
distractors: PT does not measure crack depth.
There is no magnetization in PT.
Developer color is not assessed by this check.

content.stem: Which statement about removal is correct?
options: Goal is to clear surface background while keeping penetrant in discontinuities
The goal is to remove every last bit of all the penetrant everywhere here, oddly
The goal is to add even more penetrant right down into all the openings here oddly
The whole removal step is fully optional here at all, somehow quite oddly now
content.explanation: Removal clears the surface background so indications stand out, while preserving the trapped penetrant that forms the indications.
distractors: Removing all penetrant, including from openings, would erase indications.
Removal does not add penetrant.
Removal is a required step.

content.stem: A developer performs all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Adding penetrant to the part
Blotting penetrant out of discontinuities
Providing a contrasting background
Spreading bleed-out for visibility
content.explanation: Developers draw out and spread trapped penetrant and provide contrast; they do not add penetrant to the part.
distractors: Blotting penetrant out of openings is a core developer function.
Providing contrast is a core developer function (especially for visible penetrant).
Spreading the bleed-out to magnify small indications is a developer function.

content.stem: Form a developer is:
options: Dry powder
Water-soluble
Water-suspendible
Nonaqueous (solvent-based)
content.explanation: Developer Form a is dry powder, applied to a dried surface, commonly used with fluorescent penetrant.
distractors: Water-soluble developer is Form b.
Water-suspendible developer is Form c.
Nonaqueous developers are Forms d and e.

content.stem: Form b developer is:
options: Water-soluble
Dry powder
Water-suspendible
Nonaqueous
content.explanation: Form b is a water-soluble developer dissolved in water and applied to the part, then dried.
distractors: Dry powder is Form a.
Water-suspendible is Form c.
Nonaqueous is Form d or e.

content.stem: Form c developer is:
options: Water-suspendible
Water-soluble form
A dry loose powder
A nonaqueous form
content.explanation: Form c is a water-suspendible developer where powder is suspended (not dissolved) in water, requiring agitation to keep it uniform.
distractors: Water-soluble is Form b.
Dry powder is Form a.
Nonaqueous is Form d or e.

content.stem: Forms d and e developers are:
options: Nonaqueous (solvent-based), for fluorescent and for visible penetrant respectively
Both just plain dry, loose developer powders here, somehow quite oddly enough now so
Both fully water-soluble developer types here, somehow quite oddly enough now
Both just plain emulsifier removers here, somehow quite oddly enough now indeed
content.explanation: Nonaqueous developer Form d is formulated for fluorescent (Type 1) penetrant and Form e for visible (Type 2); both are applied as solvent-suspended sprays to a dry surface.
distractors: Forms d and e are nonaqueous sprays, not dry powders.
They are solvent-based, not water-soluble.
They are developers, not emulsifiers.

content.stem: Nonaqueous developer generally provides:
options: The highest sensitivity of the developer forms for fine cracks
The very lowest overall sensitivity of them all here, quite oddly
No real contrast at all on it here, somehow quite oddly enough
Full deep subsurface defect detection here, quite oddly enough
content.explanation: Nonaqueous (solvent) developers form a fine, even film that gives strong blotting and contrast, typically the most sensitive developer form for fine surface cracks.
distractors: Nonaqueous developer is high, not low, in sensitivity.
It provides strong contrast, not none.
No developer enables subsurface detection.

content.stem: Dry powder developer is most commonly used with:
options: Fluorescent penetrant
Visible penetrant only
No penetrant
Solvent remover
content.explanation: Dry powder is typically paired with fluorescent penetrant; it clings to bleed-out areas and is light enough not to mask fluorescent indications.
distractors: Dry powder is not limited to visible penetrant and is in fact common with fluorescent.
Developer is always used with penetrant.
Dry powder is a developer, not a remover.

content.stem: Dry powder developer must be applied to a surface that is:
options: Dry
Wet
Oily
Coated with penetrant
content.explanation: Dry powder requires a dry surface so it forms an even film; moisture causes clumping and uneven coverage.
distractors: A wet surface clumps the powder.
An oily surface prevents proper powder adhesion and contaminates results.
Excess penetrant must be removed before developer is applied.

content.stem: A water-suspendible (Form c) developer bath requires agitation because:
options: The powder is suspended, not dissolved, and would settle
It is highly flammable stuff here, somehow quite oddly now
It is fully magnetic itself here, somehow quite oddly now
It emits its own UV-A light here, somehow quite oddly now
content.explanation: Suspended particles settle without agitation, changing concentration and coverage, so the bath is kept agitated for uniform application.
distractors: Water-based developer is not the flammability concern; solvent developer is.
Developers are not magnetic.
Developers do not emit UV.

content.stem: Nonaqueous developers require ventilation and fire precautions because they:
options: Use flammable solvent carriers
They contain just plain water here
They are fully magnetic themselves
They emit their own UV-A light
content.explanation: The solvent carrier in nonaqueous developers is typically flammable and emits vapors, so flash point and ventilation are managed.
distractors: Nonaqueous developers are solvent-based, not water-based.
Developers are not magnetic.
Developers do not emit UV.

content.stem: Developers improve detectability partly by 'magnifying' an indication, meaning the developer:
options: Spreads the bleed-out wider than the opening so it is easier to see
It physically enlarges the whole crack itself here, quite oddly
It adds even more red dye onto it here, somehow quite oddly now
It uses a small magnifying glass lens here, somehow quite oddly enough
content.explanation: The developer draws penetrant out and spreads it, so the visible mark is wider than the actual opening, helping the eye detect small discontinuities.
distractors: The developer does not enlarge the physical crack.
It does not add dye; the penetrant carries the dye.
Magnification here is by spreading bleed-out, not an optical lens.

content.stem: For visible penetrant, the developer's white film primarily provides:
options: A contrasting background for the colored indication
Its own bright UV-A light emission here, oddly
Full magnetic field shielding here, somehow oddly so
Full electrical current insulation here, oddly
content.explanation: The white developer contrasts with the red bleed-out under white light, making indications stand out.
distractors: Developers do not emit UV; that is the fluorescent dye's behavior.
Developers do not provide magnetic shielding.
Electrical insulation is irrelevant to PT.

content.stem: Too thick a developer coating can:
options: Mask small indications under excess powder/film
Greatly improve the overall sensitivity here too
Greatly speed up the whole bleed-out here oddly
Greatly lower the whole red background here oddly
content.explanation: An overly heavy developer layer buries faint bleed-out, so a thin uniform film is applied to preserve small-indication visibility.
distractors: Excess thickness reduces, not improves, sensitivity.
A heavy coat does not speed bleed-out and can hinder it.
Excess developer does not specifically lower meaningful background; it masks indications.

content.stem: The correct developer coating is:
options: Thin and uniform
Thick and patchy
Wet and pooled
Absent
content.explanation: A thin, uniform developer film gives the best balance of contrast, blotting, and visibility of fine indications.
distractors: A thick patchy coat masks indications and gives uneven contrast.
Pooled wet developer is uneven and can mask indications.
A developer is required; absence prevents bleed-out viewing.

content.stem: Development time exists so that:
options: Trapped penetrant has time to bleed out and spread into a visible indication
The dry developer can fully dry the red penetrant in all the openings here now
The whole entire part can be fully cleaned off here, quite oddly enough
The red penetrant dye can be fully applied on here, quite oddly enough
content.explanation: After developer is applied, time is allowed for penetrant to bleed and form indications; fine indications may need the full development time to appear.
distractors: Development draws penetrant out; it does not dry penetrant into the openings.
Cleaning is a separate step.
Penetrant application precedes developing.

content.stem: Leaving developer on far longer than specified can cause:
options: Indications to over-bleed and blur together
Indications to vanish away instantly here
The whole entire part to magnetize up here
The dry developer to become red penetrant here
content.explanation: Excessive development time lets bleed-out spread and merge, blurring indications and complicating interpretation, so viewing occurs within the window.
distractors: Indications spread rather than vanish instantly.
There is no magnetization in PT.
Developer does not convert into penetrant.

content.stem: With fluorescent penetrant, which developer is often chosen for highest sensitivity?
options: Nonaqueous Form d
A heavy aqueous Form b
No developer
A visible-only Form e
content.explanation: Nonaqueous Form d gives a fine film and strong blotting for high sensitivity with fluorescent penetrant; it is formulated for Type 1.
distractors: A heavy aqueous coat tends to reduce sensitivity versus a fine nonaqueous film.
A developer is required.
Form e is formulated for visible penetrant, not fluorescent.

content.stem: With visible penetrant, the nonaqueous developer used is:
options: Form e
Form d
Dry powder only
An emulsifier
content.explanation: Nonaqueous Form e is formulated for visible (Type 2) penetrant, providing the white contrast film under white light.
distractors: Form d is the nonaqueous developer for fluorescent penetrant.
Dry powder is one option but the nonaqueous form for visible penetrant is Form e.
An emulsifier is a removal material, not a developer.

content.stem: Dry powder developer is applied by:
options: A gentle cloud, dust chamber, or electrostatic application
Pouring it all on really heavily here, somehow quite oddly now
Spraying plain water all over it here, somehow quite oddly now
Wiping it all down with wet solvent here, somehow quite oddly
content.explanation: Dry powder is applied as a light, even cloud (often in a dust chamber or by electrostatic spray) so it lightly coats the surface and bleed-out areas.
distractors: Heavy pouring gives uneven, masking coverage.
Water is not used to apply dry powder.
Solvent wiping is a removal step, not developer application.

content.stem: The difference between water-soluble (Form b) and water-suspendible (Form c) developers is that:
options: Soluble dissolves in water; suspendible is particles held in suspension
They are both exactly fully identical here, somehow quite oddly enough
The soluble form is just a dry, loose powder here, somehow quite oddly so
The suspendible form is fully solvent-based here, quite oddly enough
content.explanation: Form b dissolves fully in water, while Form c is a powder suspended in water that must be agitated to stay uniform.
distractors: They differ in how the developer is carried in water.
Soluble developer is dissolved in water, not a dry powder.
Suspendible developer is water-based, not solvent-based.

content.stem: After an aqueous developer is applied, the part is:
options: Dried to leave a developer film
Left fully wet for inspection here
Fully re-penetrated all again here
Fully magnetized up first here
content.explanation: Water-based developers are dried so a thin developer film remains to provide contrast and blotting before inspection.
distractors: Inspection occurs after the film is dried and indications form.
Penetrant is not reapplied.
There is no magnetization in PT.

content.stem: Some high-sensitivity fluorescent procedures allow a 'no developer' inspection. This works because:
options: Strong bleed-out can be seen under UV without a developer film, where qualified
The dry developers are simply never ever useful at all here, quite oddly now
It somehow detects the deep buried subsurface defects too here, quite oddly now
The red penetrant is fully unnecessary here, somehow quite oddly enough now
content.explanation: Where qualified, very bright fluorescent penetrant can be viewed without developer, though most applications use a developer to maximize sensitivity and contrast.
distractors: Developers are generally useful and usually required.
No technique gives PT subsurface detection.
Penetrant is always required.

content.stem: Contaminated or caked developer should be:
options: Replaced, since it gives uneven coverage and poor contrast
Just fully used right up until it is empty here, quite oddly
Just mixed in with the red penetrant here, quite oddly enough
Just heated up and reused over again here, quite oddly enough
content.explanation: Developer that is contaminated, clumped, or out of condition gives unreliable coverage and is replaced to maintain consistent results.
distractors: Using degraded developer compromises results.
Developer is not mixed with penetrant.
Heating does not restore caked developer.

content.stem: The blotting action of a developer refers to its ability to:
options: Absorb and draw penetrant from the opening to the surface
Just soak up plain water only off it here, quite oddly enough
Just fully repel the red penetrant away here, quite oddly
Just fully dissolve the whole part away here, quite oddly enough
content.explanation: Developer acts like a blotter, absorbing trapped penetrant and pulling it out where it spreads and becomes visible.
distractors: It draws out penetrant, not merely water.
It attracts, not repels, penetrant.
Developer does not dissolve the part.

content.stem: Fine developer particle size helps by:
options: Forming a smooth film that resolves small indications
Just masking all the small indications here, quite oddly
Just adding color to the fluorescent dye here oddly
Just magnetizing the whole part surface here oddly
content.explanation: Fine particles create an even film with good blotting and resolution of small bleed-outs, improving detectability.
distractors: Fine particles improve, not mask, indication visibility.
Developer does not add color to fluorescent dye.
Developers do not magnetize the surface.

content.stem: Aqueous developers are often chosen for:
options: High-volume processing of many parts on a line
Quick portable field spot checks only here, oddly
Fully eliminating the whole drying step here oddly
Deep subsurface defect inspection here, oddly
content.explanation: Water-based developers suit immersion or flow-on processing of large quantities; field spot work more often uses nonaqueous aerosol developer.
distractors: Portable spot checks typically use nonaqueous aerosol developer.
Aqueous developers still require a drying step.
No developer enables subsurface inspection.

content.stem: Watching how quickly penetrant bleeds into the developer helps distinguish:
options: A strong, fast-bleeding crack from faint non-relevant marks
The exact UV-A light wavelength used here, quite oddly enough
The whole part's overall magnetism level here, quite oddly enough
The red penetrant's exact flash point here, quite oddly enough
content.explanation: The speed and strength of bleed-out into the developer gives interpretation clues about the discontinuity, separating relevant from non-relevant indications.
distractors: Bleed rate does not reveal UV wavelength.
There is no magnetism in PT.
Flash point is a safety property, unrelated to bleed observation.

content.stem: Uniform developer coverage is important so that:
options: Indications appear consistently across the whole area
Only a small part of the surface develops here oddly
The whole entire part dries out much faster here oddly
The whole red penetrant is fully removed off here oddly
content.explanation: Even coverage ensures bleed-out is drawn out and contrasted uniformly, so no area is left with weak or no development.
distractors: Partial development leaves areas unexamined.
Coverage uniformity is about indication formation, not drying speed.
Developer draws penetrant out; it does not remove it from openings.

content.stem: Nonaqueous developer aerosol should be sprayed:
options: From an appropriate distance to deposit a thin, even film
Up real close to fully pool it all on here, quite oddly enough
Right onto a fully soaking wet surface here, quite oddly enough
Well before any red penetrant has even been applied here oddly
content.explanation: Spraying from the correct distance gives a light uniform coat; spraying too close pools the developer and can mask indications.
distractors: Close spraying pools developer and masks indications.
Nonaqueous developer goes on a dried surface.
Developer always follows penetrant and removal.

content.stem: The three main roles of a developer are to:
options: Blot penetrant out, spread/magnify it, and provide contrast
To magnetize, demagnetize, and then clean it here oddly
To apply the couplant, send a pulse, and read the echo here too
To expose, then process, and then view the whole film here
content.explanation: Developers draw penetrant from openings, spread it to magnify small indications, and provide a contrasting background.
distractors: Magnetize/demagnetize/clean describes magnetic methods, not developer roles.
Couple/pulse/echo is ultrasonic terminology.
Expose/process/view is radiographic terminology.

content.stem: Dry powder developer is favored with fluorescent penetrant partly because it:
options: Does not add a heavy white film that would dilute the fluorescent glow
It emits its very own UV-A light here, somehow quite oddly enough
It is fully solvent-based itself here, somehow quite oddly enough
It fully removes the red penetrant off here, somehow quite oddly enough
content.explanation: A light dry powder lets the fluorescent indication glow clearly, whereas a heavy white film could dilute the visible glow; nonaqueous Form d is also common for high sensitivity.
distractors: Developers do not emit UV.
Dry powder is not solvent-based.
Developer draws penetrant out, it does not remove it from openings.

content.stem: Developer materials should be stored:
options: Sealed and dry to prevent moisture absorption and caking
Left wide open to the humid damp air here, quite oddly enough
Mixed in with the red penetrant here, somehow quite oddly now
In direct hot sunlight while left wide open here, oddly
content.explanation: Keeping developer sealed and dry prevents moisture uptake that causes caking and uneven application.
distractors: Humid air causes caking of dry developer.
Developer is stored separately from penetrant.
Open exposure to sunlight and air degrades developer.

content.stem: Aqueous developer concentration is controlled because too concentrated a mix can:
options: Leave a heavy film that masks indications
Improve sensitivity without any real limit
Emit its own bright UV-A light here
Magnetize the whole entire part here oddly
content.explanation: Over-concentration produces a thick film that buries small indications, so concentration is checked and maintained per the specification.
distractors: Higher concentration does not endlessly improve sensitivity; it can mask indications.
Developer does not emit UV.
There is no magnetization in PT.

content.stem: Which developer-form mapping is correct?
options: a: dry; b: water-soluble; c: water-suspendible; d/e: nonaqueous
a: nonaqueous; b: dry powder; c: solvent; d: plain water, oddly
All of the forms are just plain dry powder here, quite oddly enough
All of the forms are fully nonaqueous based here, quite oddly enough
content.explanation: Form a is dry powder, b is water-soluble, c is water-suspendible, and d and e are nonaqueous (for fluorescent and visible respectively).
distractors: This option scrambles the developer-form mapping.
The forms are not all dry powder.
The forms are not all nonaqueous.

content.stem: A common error is applying developer:
options: Before adequately removing surface penetrant, causing heavy background
Well after the whole postcleaning step is fully done here, oddly
Well before any precleaning of the whole part here, quite oddly
Right instead of the red penetrant itself here, quite oddly enough also
content.explanation: Developing over un-removed surface penetrant floods the surface with background; developer must follow proper excess removal.
distractors: Developer is applied before, not after, postcleaning.
Precleaning is the first step; developer comes much later.
Developer supplements, not replaces, penetrant.

content.stem: Nonaqueous developers dry quickly because:
options: The volatile solvent carrier evaporates rapidly, leaving the film
They simply contain plain water in them here, quite oddly enough
They are fully heated up red hot here, somehow quite oddly enough
They are fully magnetic themselves here, somehow quite oddly enough
content.explanation: The solvent carrier flashes off quickly, depositing a fine developer film and starting bleed-out promptly.
distractors: Nonaqueous developers are solvent-based, not water-based.
They dry by solvent evaporation, not applied heat.
They are not magnetic.

content.stem: For very tight cracks, the developer is especially important because it:
options: Pulls out the small amount of penetrant and spreads it to a visible width
It physically widens the whole open crack itself here, quite oddly enough
It adds even more red penetrant right into it here, quite oddly enough
It fully cools the whole entire part right down here, quite oddly enough

distractors: The developer does not physically widen the crack.
It draws out existing penetrant; it does not add more.
Cooling the part is not a developer function.

content.stem: Indications should be evaluated:
options: Within the specified development time window
Only after the dry developer is fully removed
Well before any dry developer is applied here
Several whole days later on here oddly
content.explanation: Evaluation occurs during/after development within the specified window, before over-bleed blurs indications or the developer is cleaned off.
distractors: Removing developer ends the inspection; evaluation comes first.
Indications form with the developer, not before it.
Waiting days lets indications over-bleed and the developer degrade.

content.stem: A properly developed visible-penetrant surface appears:
options: Uniformly white with indications standing out in color
All patchy and bare all over here, somehow quite oddly now
All brightly glowing under the UV-A black light here oddly
All fully wet and dripping all over here, quite oddly now
content.explanation: A good visible-penetrant developer film is an even white background against which colored indications are clearly visible.
distractors: Patchy bare areas indicate poor developer coverage.
Glowing under UV describes fluorescent inspection, not visible.
A dripping surface indicates the developer was not properly applied or dried.

content.stem: Which statement about developers is correct?
options: Nonaqueous developer generally gives the highest sensitivity for fine cracks
The dry developers somehow add more penetrant onto the whole part here, oddly
The dry developers somehow fully magnetize the whole entire part here, oddly now
The dry developers are simply fully optional in every single case here, oddly
content.explanation: Among developer forms, nonaqueous typically offers the highest sensitivity for fine surface cracks due to its fine, even film and strong blotting.
distractors: Developers draw out penetrant; they do not add it.
Developers do not magnetize the part.
A developer is required in most qualified procedures.

content.stem: Fluorescent penetrant inspection uses light in the:
options: UV-A range, near 365 nm
The UV-C germicidal range
The far infrared range
The microwave band range
content.explanation: UV-A near 365 nm excites the fluorescent dye to emit visible light; UV-C is hazardous and not used for inspection.
distractors: UV-C is germicidal and unsafe for inspection use.
Infrared does not excite the fluorescent dye.
Microwaves are not used in PT.

content.stem: Minimum UV-A irradiance at the part surface for fluorescent PT is commonly:
options: 1000 microwatts per square centimeter
Only 100 microwatts per square centimeter
10 microwatts per square centimeter
1 microwatt per square centimeter
content.explanation: A common requirement is at least 1000 microwatts/cm-squared UV-A at the examination surface, verified with a radiometer.
distractors: 100 microwatts/cm-squared is below the standard minimum.
10 microwatts/cm-squared is far too low.
1 microwatt/cm-squared is negligible for excitation.

content.stem: During fluorescent PT, ambient white light at the inspection surface should not exceed about:
options: 2 foot-candles (about 20 lux)
100 foot-candles (about 1000 lux)
50 foot-candles (about 500 lux)
200 lux (about 20 foot-candles)
content.explanation: Ambient white light is kept low, commonly 2 foot-candles (about 20 lux) or less, so faint fluorescent indications remain visible.

50 foot-candles is far too bright for fluorescent inspection.
